# Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI {.unnumbered} Cleaning is where an AI assistant looks most useful and where its mistakes are hardest to see. A cleaning script can run without error, return the right columns and produce plausible values while having treated a missing-value code as a measurement, kept the same animal twice, or dropped a row nobody noticed. None of these raises an error. This block treats cleaning as four artefacts, each with a different owner: | Artefact | Owner | Why | |---|---|---| | Codebook (`docs/codebook.csv`) | You | Missing-value codes, units, valid ranges and label mappings are facts about how the data were collected. They cannot be inferred reliably from the values. | | Cleaning skill | Reusable | *How* you clean: never touch raw data, log every change, never drop a row silently. The same for every dataset. | | Validation and audit scripts | You, or a separate AI conversation | Written from the codebook, independently of the cleaning code, so one misunderstanding cannot pass both. | | Enforcement | Configuration | Rules that hold whether or not the agent follows its instructions. | The codebookA table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI. is the hub. The cleaning and the checks both read it, but neither reads the other, so a misunderstanding in one is caught by the other: :::::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="The cleaning pipeline and its owners. The raw data are pinned by a checksum and profiled with R. You write the codebook from the profile and the data provider's note. Two independent branches read the codebook: the AI cleans with the skill, writing scripts/01_clean.R, the clean data and the cleaning and exclusion logs; the validation rules are transcribed from the codebook separately. The tests and the audit then compare the raw data, the clean data and the logs."} ::::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Facts first ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} `data/raw/voles_raw.csv`, pinned by a checksum ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} profiled in R ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-plain} `00_profile.R` output ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} plus the provider's note ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} `docs/codebook.csv` ::: ::::::: ::::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Two branches that read the codebook, never each other ::: :::::: {.dia-branches} ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Skill writes and runs `scripts/01_clean.R` ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} writes ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} Clean data, cleaning log, exclusion log ::: ::::: ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Validation rules in `validate_voles.R`, transcribed from the codebook ::: ::::: :::::: ::::::: ::::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Then compare ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} Tests and audit: raw data unchanged, every row accounted for, every change logged ::: ::::::: ::: {.dia-caption} Independence is the point: one misunderstanding cannot pass both branches. ::: :::::::: You will work on a version of the voles data with errors planted in it. Your instructor holds the answer key, so at the end you can measure what your pipeline caught and what it missed. *⏱ ~54 minutes* :::{.callout-note} **Why not simply ask the AI to clean the data?** In a 2025 study, language models given deliberately polluted tables found missing values in standard formats but struggled with codes such as `-1` (a sentinel valueA number with a special meaning, such as 9999 for “not recorded” or -1 for “run failed”. It must be documented in a codebook and recoded before analysis.), rarely detected non-exact duplicates, and did worse as errors increased (Spreafico et al., 2025). The models were older than those you will use and did not write or run code, so treat this as a map of where to look. Those error classes are planted in this block's data. ::: ## The repository layout This is the part of [your workshop repository](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd) that Block 7 uses: ``` .agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md the skill .claude/ ├── settings.json the deny rules, from Block 6 └── skills/clean-with-codebook/ a copy of the skill folder above .gitattributes stops line-ending changes to raw data data/ ├── raw/voles_raw.csv never edited by anyone └── derived/ cleaning outputs and logs docs/ ├── data_note.md the data provider's note └── codebook.csv you write this in Step 2 scripts/ ├── 00_profile.R provided ├── 01_clean.R written by the agent in Step 4 ├── 02_validate.R provided ├── 03_audit_cleaning.R provided └── functions/validate_voles.R provided tests/ ├── fixtures/raw_checksum.txt you create this in Step 0 └── test_cleaning.R provided ``` If your workshop repository does not already contain `.agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/`, download the skill and unzip it into `.agents/skills/`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Claude Code reads skills from `.claude/skills/`, so copy the `clean-with-codebook` folder there as well, so that `.claude/skills/clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md` exists. (On macOS or Linux you can use a symbolic link instead, as in [Block 5](11e-instructions-skills.qmd).) :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Posit Assistant reads `.agents/skills/` directly, so no copy is needed. ::: ## Step 0: Lock the raw data Everything later depends on the raw file being exactly what the data provider sent. The deny rules from [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) already protect it; here you add a checksumA short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route. and confirm the rules work. **1. Record a checksum and commit it.** Run this once, yourself. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_path <- here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") checksum_path <- here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt") writeLines(unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)), checksum_path) ``` ::: Then commit `tests/fixtures/raw_checksum.txt`. **2. Confirm the deny rules are active.** In Claude Code, run `/permissions`. The rules from `.claude/settings.json` should be listed, including the deny ruleA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. `Edit(/data/raw/**)`. **3. Test the control, do not assume it.** Ask: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Add a comment line to the top of data/raw/voles_raw.csv. ``` It should be refused. Then confirm the file is unchanged. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} identical(unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)), readLines(checksum_path)) ``` ::: R returns `TRUE`. (The full test file in Step 5 also checks this, but its other tests need the cleaned data, which do not exist yet.) The deny rule prevents one route; the checksum detects a change made by any route. *Going further* lists the full settings file and what each control covers. ## Step 1: Profile the raw data (R, not AI) Profiling is counting, and counting is something you should compute rather than ask a model to estimate. Run the provided script yourself, in the R console or with `Rscript scripts/00_profile.R` in the terminal: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/00_profile.R ---- # Purpose: describe the raw file as entered, before any decision is made. # Every column is read as character so codes such as 9999 or -1 appear # exactly as entered. library(tidyverse) library(here) raw_df <- read_csv( here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()) ) # one row per column: missingness, distinct values, numeric range ---- profile_df <- raw_df |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |> # suppressWarnings: text values become NA here by design mutate(value_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value))) |> summarise( n_rows = n(), n_missing = sum(is.na(value)), n_distinct = n_distinct(value, na.rm = TRUE), n_numeric = sum(!is.na(value_num)), min_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else min(value_num, na.rm = TRUE), max_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else max(value_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = column ) # every distinct label in the categorical columns ---- labels_df <- raw_df |> select(sex, treatment_arm) |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |> count(column, value, sort = TRUE) # identifiers that appear more than once ---- repeated_ids_df <- raw_df |> count(subject_id) |> filter(n > 1) print(profile_df, n = Inf) print(labels_df, n = Inf) print(repeated_ids_df) ``` ::: Keep the output. It is the factual input to Step 2. ## Step 2: Draft the codebook, then audit it The codebook is the data dictionary you wrote for the README on Day 2 ([Fixing it with structure, cleaning and a README](06-reproducibility.qmd#repro-fix)), with machine-readable rules added: valid ranges, missing-value codes and label mappings that both the cleaning skill and the validation rules can read. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Draft and audit the codebook (12 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Let an AI draft it from the profile alone.** Use a browser chat window, not Claude Code: started in your workshop repository, Claude Code could open `docs/data_note.md` itself, and the point of this step is to see what the AI infers without it. Paste only the profile output. **Prompt (browser chat):** ```text Here is a profile of a raw data file. Draft a codebook as CSV with the columns: column, type, rule, min, max, missing_codes, unit, source. In the source column, state for every entry whether it comes from the profile or is your assumption. [paste the output of scripts/00_profile.R] ``` Save the draft as `docs/codebook.csv` yourself. The deny rules stop the agent from writing that file: the codebook is yours. **2. Audit the draft.** Before you open `docs/data_note.md`, answer: - Did the draft list `9999` as a missing-value code, or treat it as a large measurement? - Did it notice that `-1` is a code? - Where did its `min` and `max` come from? A range read off the data includes the errors in the data, so it cannot be used to detect them. Valid ranges must come from the biology or the protocol. **3. Correct it against the data provider's note.** Open `docs/data_note.md` and edit the codebook yourself. Every line should be traceable to the note or to a decision you can defend. Commit it. :::: :::
``` column,type,rule,min,max,missing_codes,unit,source subject_id,character,"pattern ^V[0-9]{3}$; unique; pad digits to three",,,,,data note sex,character,"allowed M, F; recode male to M, female to F",,,,,data note treatment_arm,character,"allowed Control, Low_dose, High_dose; match case-insensitively",,,,,data note mass_pre_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records) mass_post_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records) metabolic_rate_post,double,,5,30,-1,,data note (range from equipment) ```
## Step 3: Run the validation rules Validation rules are transcribed from the codebook, not from the cleaning script. If the same AI conversation writes both, a single misunderstanding (for example, that `-1` is a valid reading) passes both. The template provides `scripts/functions/validate_voles.R`, written from the codebook by a person. It uses the pointblank package: each line is one rule, and `interrogate()` reports how many rows break it. (pointblank calls the object that holds the rules an "agent"; it has nothing to do with AI agents.) You do not need to write pointblank code today.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/validate_voles.R ---- # Rules transcribed from docs/codebook.csv by a human, not by the agent # that writes the cleaning script. voles_col_types <- function() { readr::cols( subject_id = readr::col_character(), sex = readr::col_character(), treatment_arm = readr::col_character(), mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(), mass_post_g = readr::col_double(), metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double(), .default = readr::col_character() ) } validate_voles <- function(data, label) { data |> pointblank::create_agent(label = label) |> pointblank::col_vals_not_null(columns = c(subject_id, sex, treatment_arm)) |> pointblank::col_vals_regex(columns = subject_id, regex = "^V[0-9]{3}$") |> pointblank::rows_distinct(columns = subject_id) |> pointblank::col_vals_in_set(columns = sex, set = c("M", "F")) |> pointblank::col_vals_in_set( columns = treatment_arm, set = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose") ) |> pointblank::col_vals_between( columns = c(mass_pre_g, mass_post_g), left = 15, right = 60, na_pass = TRUE ) |> pointblank::col_vals_between( columns = metabolic_rate_post, left = 5, right = 30, na_pass = TRUE ) |> pointblank::interrogate() } ``` :::
**Run the rules on the raw data. They should fail.** If raw data pass every rule, either the data are already clean or the rules are too weak, and you should suspect the second. Run the provided `scripts/02_validate.R` in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/02_validate.R ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R")) raw_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) validate_voles(raw_df, "Raw data: expected to FAIL") ``` ::: Note which rules fail and how many rows each flags. Every failure is a problem that the cleaning must resolve or log. :::{.callout-warning} `na_pass = TRUE` lets genuine missing values through. It would also let through a cleaning script that replaced *every* mass with `NA`. Validation alone cannot catch over-cleaning; the audit in Step 5 can. ::: ## Step 4: Clean with the skill, plan first The skill holds the procedure; the codebook holds the facts. It sets `disable-model-invocation: true`, so it runs only when you invoke it by name. That is appropriate for a workflow that writes files. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `.agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` markdown --- name: clean-with-codebook description: >- Writes or revises a reproducible R cleaning script that applies a human-authored codebook (docs/codebook.csv) to raw tabular data. Use when asked to clean, recode or prepare raw data in a project that has a codebook. Not for exploratory analysis or modelling. disable-model-invocation: true --- # Clean data against a codebook ## Hard constraints 1. Never modify anything under data/raw/. Read raw files with explicit column types. 2. The codebook is the only source of rules. Do not infer units, ranges, missing-value codes or label mappings that the codebook does not state. 3. Do not edit docs/, scripts/functions/, scripts/02_validate.R, scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R or anything under tests/. If a check fails, report it; never change a check to make it pass. 4. Never drop a row silently. Every excluded row goes in the exclusion log with a reason. 5. Every changed cell goes in the cleaning log. 6. A value outside a codebook range that no codebook rule explains is set to NA, logged with rule "out_of_range_query", and listed in the final report. Never correct it by guessing a unit or decimal error. 7. No imputation. 8. Tidyverse style, native pipe, here::here() for all paths. ## Procedure 1. Present a plan before writing anything: every rule you will apply, the codebook row it comes from, and the order. Wait for the user to confirm. 2. If the data contain a value the codebook does not cover, stop and ask. 3. Write scripts/01_clean.R and run it in a fresh R session. 4. Run scripts/02_validate.R on the clean data and run the tests in tests/. Report the results verbatim. ## Outputs (exact columns) - data/derived/voles_clean.csv: the codebook columns plus raw_row, the row number in the raw file. - data/derived/exclusion_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, reason. - data/derived/cleaning_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, column, old_value, new_value, rule. ## Final report Row counts in, out and excluded; every value set to NA for query; any gaps in the codebook you found. ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Plan, review, then execute (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Start in plan mode and invoke the skill.** With your repository committed and clean, start Claude Code in `plan` mode (`Shift+Tab` until the mode shows `plan`, or `claude --permission-mode plan`), then: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text /clean-with-codebook Clean data/raw/voles_raw.csv using docs/codebook.csv. Start with the plan. ``` :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Switch to plan mode with `/plan`, then invoke the skill with the same prompt. ::: **2. Review the plan before approving it.** Check that: - every rule cites a codebook row; - out-of-range values are set to `NA` and queried, not "corrected"; - no file outside `scripts/01_clean.R` and `data/derived/` will be written; - duplicates are handled by a stated rule, with each exclusion logged. **3. Approve, and keep approving each step.** When Claude Code asks how to proceed, choose **Yes, manually approve edits**, so it still asks before each change (see the [quick reference](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd#cc-quick-reference)). Read each request, and note every time it stopped to ask you something. A well-behaved agent should stop at least once. :::: ::: ## Step 5: Check the result Five checks, each catching something the others cannot. **1. Validation on clean data should pass.** **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R")) clean_df <- readr::read_csv( here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types() ) validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data: expected to pass") ``` ::: **2. The tests: raw data unchanged and every row accounted for.** The provided `tests/test_cleaning.R`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/test_cleaning.R ---- library(testthat) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R")) read_chr <- function(...) { readr::read_csv( here::here(...), col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character()) ) } test_that("raw data are unchanged", { recorded <- readLines(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")) current <- unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"))) expect_identical(current, recorded) }) test_that("every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log", { raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv") excluded_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "exclusion_log.csv") expect_equal(nrow(raw_df), nrow(clean_df) + nrow(excluded_df)) expect_setequal( c(clean_df$raw_row, excluded_df$raw_row), as.character(seq_len(nrow(raw_df))) ) expect_false(any(is.na(excluded_df$reason) | excluded_df$reason == "")) }) test_that("clean data pass every codebook rule", { clean_df <- readr::read_csv( here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types() ) validation <- validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data") expect_true(pointblank::all_passed(validation)) }) ``` ::: In the R console, run `testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_cleaning.R"))`. **3. Audit the logs against the data.** The cleaning log was written by the agent, so check it rather than trust it. Run the provided `scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R` in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R")) to_long <- function(data, value_name) { data |> pivot_longer( -raw_row, names_to = "column", values_to = value_name, values_transform = as.character ) } raw_long_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) |> mutate(raw_row = as.character(row_number())) |> to_long("raw_value") clean_long_df <- read_csv(here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) |> to_long("clean_value") cleaning_log_df <- read_csv( here("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()) ) # 1. Truthful: every logged old value matches the raw file ---- untruthful_df <- cleaning_log_df |> left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |> filter(!map2_lgl(old_value, raw_value, identical)) # 2. Complete: every changed cell appears in the log ---- unlogged_df <- clean_long_df |> left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |> filter(!map2_lgl(clean_value, raw_value, identical)) |> anti_join(cleaning_log_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) untruthful_df unlogged_df # 3. What kinds of change were made ---- cleaning_log_df |> count(column, rule, sort = TRUE) # 4. Ten logged changes to check by hand against the raw file ---- set.seed(2026) cleaning_log_df |> slice_sample(n = 10) ``` ::: `untruthful_df` and `unlogged_df` should both have zero rows. An unlogged change is the most dangerous outcome in this block: a value altered with no record. If a row appears, inspect it; a difference in number formatting is harmless, a changed value is not. For the ten sampled changes, open the raw file yourself and confirm each one. **4. Reproduce it without the agent.** Your `AGENTS.md` and the skill asked for a script that runs in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work, such as the one Rscript starts. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record. with the packages in the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment., `renv.lock`. Check, rather than trust. Commit the outputs, then: **In the terminal:** ```bash Rscript -e "renv::status()" Rscript scripts/01_clean.R git status --short data/derived ``` `renv::status()` should report that the project is in a consistent state. If the agent installed or used a package that is not in `renv.lock`, it says so; decide whether you want the package, then update the lockfile with `renv::snapshot()` as on [Day 1](01-projects.qmd). `Rscript` runs the script in a fresh R session, and the same script on the same raw data must write the same outputs, so `git status` should show no changes. If a derived file changed, the cleaning is not deterministic: find out why before going on. **5. Grade the pipeline against the planted errors.** Your instructor will now release the answer key. For each planted error, record: | Planted error | Failed validation on raw? | Handled as intended? | In the log? | |---|---|---|---| | | | | | The first column measures your *rules*; the second measures the *cleaning*; the third measures the *record*. A planted error that passed validation on raw data is a hole in your codebook, whatever the cleaning did. ## Debrief 1. Which planted errors did the AI's first draft of the codebook miss before you gave it the data provider's note? What does that say about who should own the codebook? 2. What did the agent do with the mass recorded in kilograms and the value ten times too large? If it "corrected" them, on whose authority? If the provider confirms a kilogram entry, the correction becomes a codebook rule you add, not something the script infers. 3. Which of your checks would have caught a script that set every mass to `NA`? **Payoff.** What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again? :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **Check:** validation rules transcribed from the codebook, not from the cleaning code; tests; the log audited against the raw file; the answer key. - **Reproduce:** `renv::status()` and a fresh `Rscript` run that writes identical outputs. Once the clean output is right, you can freeze it as a reference, as you will in [Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd), so a later refactor of `01_clean.R` must reproduce it exactly. - **Record:** the codebook, the cleaning and exclusion logs, and a line in `docs/ai-log.md`: the skill, how many planted errors were handled as intended, and anything you overrode. ::: ## Check your understanding **Why must the codebook be written or confirmed by the analyst rather than inferred by the AI from the data?**
**Your validation rules all pass on the raw data before any cleaning. What is the most likely explanation in this exercise?**
**How does the checksum test differ from the deny rule?**
## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ### The Step 0 controls in full **Line endings.** The template's `.gitattributes` contains this line, so git does not convert line endings, which would change the checksum on Windows: ``` data/raw/** -text ``` **Deny rules.** This is the `.claude/settings.json` in your workshop repository, the same file you read in [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd): ```json { "permissions": { "deny": [ "Edit(/data/raw/**)", "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)", "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)", "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)", "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)", "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)", "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)", "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)", "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)", "Edit(/.github/**)", "Edit(/.claude/**)", "Edit(/.posit/**)", "Edit(/hooks/**)", "Read(/.Renviron)", "Read(/.env)" ] } } ``` A leading `/` anchors each pattern to the project root. The rules protect specific files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write `scripts/01_clean.R` and `data/derived/`. Posit Assistant has no documented path rules for file edits; use the guard hook from the *Going further* section of [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) instead. :::{.callout-warning} **What each control covers.** The deny rule blocks the agent's file-editing tools, and shell output redirects such as `> file`. It does not cover R code the agent runs: an R script that writes to `data/raw/` is a different route. The checksum test catches a change made by *any* route, but only after the fact. On the Copilot cloud agent, where you have no local permission file, the checksum test running in CI plus branch protection is your control. Use both where you can: one prevents, the other detects. ::: **Data governance.** A deny rule on editing does not stop data reaching the model provider; see [Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd). ### Write the validation rules independently Instead of using the provided `validate_voles.R`, you can have the rules written by an AI that has never seen the cleaning code, for example a browser chat window given only the codebook: **Prompt (browser chat):** ```text Using only the codebook below, write an R file containing a function validate_voles(data, label) that builds a pointblank agent with one validation step per codebook rule, and interrogates it. Also write voles_col_types(), returning readr column types for the codebook columns, with character as the default for anything else. [paste docs/codebook.csv] ``` Compare what it writes with the provided version in Step 3. A rule it missed, or a range it took from the data rather than the codebook, is the kind of error the separate conversation is meant to expose. ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
checksum A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route.
codebook A table describing each variable: its type, valid range, missing-value codes, unit and label mappings. It is the data dictionary from Day 2 with machine-readable rules, and you own it, not the AI.
deny rule A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.
fresh R session An R session with nothing loaded from earlier work, such as the one Rscript starts. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record.
